components: The 5 EC belong to the assessed year assignment. BAST themes embedded in other modules carry no additional separate credits.
Design and Analysis of Biomedical Studies

Published entry conditions include Human Biology, Biomolecules, Cellular Communication, Medical Genetics, Immunology, Physiology Basic Concepts and Physiology Advanced Concepts. The last prerequisite is absent from the current programme; its applicable replacement or removal remains unresolved.
Required module after completed Molecular Biology, Cellular Communication and Immunology.

Required individual supervised biomedical research. All first- and second-year examinations must be passed. Written project agreement must reach the internship committee at least four weeks before the start.
Required scientific writing, peer review and research poster; Communication in Science 1 and 2 must be completed.
Genuine 30-EC third-year choice space from 2026–2027: a full minor, half-minor with electives or project extension, or a separate elective project. Specific subjects are not compulsory.

core: Human biology from molecules and cells to tissues, organs and the whole body
Molecular cell biology, biochemistry, genetics, cell signalling and genomics
Mechanisms, causes, diagnosis, prevention and treatment of human disease
Immunology, medical microbiology and infectious disease
Experimental, laboratory and independent biomedical research
Epidemiology, biostatistics, biomedical data and research design
adjacent: Molecular diagnostics, therapeutic development and translation to clinical care
Disease prevention, public health, medical ethics and communication
questions: How do healthy and diseased human bodies function from molecules to organs?
How can genetic, cellular, immunological and experimental methods explain disease mechanisms?
How can biomedical evidence support prevention, diagnosis and improved treatment?

trace: Complementary efficiency/equity analysis, public goods, taxation, health/education expenditure and social insurance support health-policy reasoning; this is not clinical economics or biomedical mechanism training.

Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.

Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.

Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.

Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.

Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.

Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.

Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.

Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
Complementary signals, transforms, sampling, filtering and feedback support dynamic measurement/model reasoning. Actual examples are general engineering; clinical diagnostics are not promised.

Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.

Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.

Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.

Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.

Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Skeletal, thoracic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, reproductive and lower urinary anatomy are developed through spatial reasoning, medical images, anatomical drawing and human-specimen material. Guided practicals and dissection-room observation connect three-dimensional relationships to variation. Historical, ethical and societal questions about human remains, representation and sex accompany the anatomical study; activities are framed as academic learning rather than clinical qualification.

Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.

Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.

Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.

Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.

Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology. Description supports neural perception/action and cognitive-neuroscience methods without inventing a particular experiment.

Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.

Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.

Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.

Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.

Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.

Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.

Direct biochemical, microbial and molecular laboratory formation: bacterial transformation, protein purification, DNA analysis and reproducible records. Selected display description is limited to these supported methods; no unsupported extra experiment is claimed.

Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.

Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.

Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.

Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.

Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.

Complementary persuasion, framing and ethical communication methods are practised through sustainability/community projects. Health campaigning is a possible transfer, not the actual promised assessment.

alternatives.label: Human biology, disease and biomedical research
alternatives.concept: Combines molecular and cellular biology, anatomy, physiology, infection, immunity, pharmacology and disease mechanisms with laboratory work, statistics, evidence synthesis and ethics. Neuroscience adds a neural view of human illness. It approaches the biomedical core while leaving substantial differences in specialised laboratory training and compulsory independent research.
alternatives.labelReason: The official degree centres on the human body, disease mechanisms, molecular and cellular biology, microbiology, immunology, laboratory work and independent biomedical research.

All remain provisional while external progression is unresolved.

alternatives.label: Public health, disease prevention and biomedical intervention
alternatives.concept: Connects biological disease mechanisms with population patterns, prevention and intervention. Epidemiology, health psychology, sociology and qualitative research develop health-context inquiry; public economics examines health spending and policy. Laboratory, statistical and evidence-synthesis work retains a biomedical research core. Persuasion methods add communication practice through sustainability projects, rather than a promised clinical campaign.

candidates.label: Public health, disease prevention and biomedical intervention

selection.assessment: All eligible interests are assigned to the core or two coherent candidates. Three provisional curricula meet UCR implementation and quantitative/qualitative distinctness requirements. They are research findings only, not a final comparability approval while the external prerequisite rule remains unresolved.

blocks: Both develop academic information use, argument, reflection and collaboration. UCR combines these with personal development and civic engagement; Leiden’s assessed assignment addresses biomedical science and society.
Both connect human anatomical structure with function. UCR emphasises regional and system anatomy, spatial reasoning, specimens and medical images; Leiden also introduces embryology and development.

Both examine therapeutic targets and drug intervention. UCR supplies pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and antimicrobial/neural/immune applications; it does not reproduce the dedicated cancer mechanisms, tumour microenvironment and cancer-cell experiment.
Both study innate and adaptive immune mechanisms, cellular interactions, immune disease and intervention. UCR also examines infection and flow-cytometry data; Leiden has a separate infection module.

Both link organ function, disease mechanisms, symptoms, diagnostic findings and therapeutic intervention. UCR uses clinical cases and coherent pathophysiological reasoning; Leiden adds dedicated tissue pathology and anatomical practical work. External progression remains unresolved.

Both concern nervous-system biology. UCR develops comparative brain anatomy, physiology, regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms; the relation is bounded by the available current Leiden module evidence.

Both connect neural mechanisms with behaviour, dysfunction and psychoactive drugs. UCR centres higher cognitive functions and experimental design; Leiden additionally integrates endocrine cascades, stress, reproduction and gene-expression analysis.
Both introduce biological molecules, cells, membranes and their integrated functions. UCR provides broader molecular and cellular foundations rather than the same laboratory sequence.

Both study DNA replication and repair, gene expression, cell division and cell fate. UCR integrates cellular regulation and molecular therapeutic targets; Leiden includes its own developmental and experimental sequence.

Both examine cardiovascular, respiratory and renal functions, homeostasis and clinical illustrations. UCR covers the wider adult human body; it does not establish Leiden’s additional prerequisite rule.

Both develop integrated metabolic pathways, enzyme regulation and biomolecular transformations. UCR includes biochemical disease analysis; this does not cover both Leiden metabolism modules independently.
Both connect inheritance, genetic variation, molecular diagnosis and disease. UCR combines genetics with cellular pathology, neoplasia and research-proposal design.
Research orientation through a skin-cancer question has no separate selected UCR counterpart after foundations and academic skills are placed elsewhere.
Dedicated digestion, nutritional components and gastrointestinal anatomy are not represented by a separate additional UCR course.
Dedicated signalling, calcium homeostasis, bone development and receptor interactions remain additional Leiden study; the UCR cell-biology contribution is already placed at Molecular Biology.
Leiden integrates a clinical problem from molecules to populations through individual and group work. No separate selected UCR course reproduces this component.
A separate compulsory pathogens, microbiome-data and experimental infection project remains beyond the UCR immunity course already placed once.
Life-science discovery, company visits, venture building and intellectual property are not reproduced by general public economics.
The second-year integrated English writing, scientific presentation and symposium reporting sequence is not represented by an additional selected UCR course.
Interview-based investigation of daily biomedical research practice and careers is not equivalent to statistical methods or literature synthesis.

Required19EC supervised individual research, notebook, poster and report. UCR laboratory and methods courses do not establish completion; optional independent research would remain separate from the scheduled180EC.

Both use philosophical and ethical reasoning to examine difficult questions. UCR develops general moral theories and independent argument; Leiden specifically examines biomedical knowledge, scientific responsibility and research dilemmas.
An integrated year of biomedical scientific communication is not equivalent to a standalone persuasion course with sustainability projects.
Specific third-year minor, internship and future-study choice workshops have no separate scheduled UCR counterpart.
Genuine30EC open minor/elective space has no predetermined subject counterpart. No named UCR course is aligned merely to fill this space.

Both develop empirical questions, study design and statistical analysis. UCR practises survey and experimental research with R in social and behavioural contexts, while Leiden centres biomedical studies.
Both use R for data handling, visualisation and reproducible analysis. UCR extends into text and spatial data and a data-based research project.

Both develop study-design reasoning, regression, group comparisons, categorical outcomes and model checks. Leiden additionally specifies survival analysis and biomedical measurement validation; UCR applications centre health and behaviour.
Dedicated scientific article, peer review and research-poster work is integrated with third-year research and has no separate selected UCR equivalent.

notes.text: Leiden combines dedicated molecular, physiological, clinical, immune and laboratory study with a19EC Student Research Project and30EC of elective space. UCR offers related biomedical, population-health and quantitative study, with different laboratory and research commitments. The current Leiden Human Pathology entry requirement still needs clarification, so these UCR constructions remain provisional.
